title: Wear-and-Tear Charges vs. Buying Your Lease: What the Inspection Decides
description: A lease-end inspection can add excess wear and mileage charges if you return the car. Here is how the inspection works, what you can dispute, and how it changes the buy-or-return math.
body:
Most people compare a lease payoff with what the car is worth. There is a second comparison that gets less attention: what it would cost to return the car. At the end of a closed-end lease, the Federal Reserve's consumer leasing guidance lists three charges that may apply when you hand the car back: a disposition fee, excess mileage charges, and excessive wear-and-tear charges.

How the inspection works

The Fed's guide says the lessor tells you where to return the car, and the vehicle is then inspected for excessive wear and excess mileage. The inspector is typically one of four parties: a dealership affiliated with the lessor, the lessor itself, a private appraiser, or an auto auction.

What counts as excessive

Any wear the lessor's standard does not define as excessive is considered normal, and that standard is written in your lease agreement. The Fed's examples include broken or missing parts, dented or damaged body panels or trim, cuts, tears, burns or permanent stains in the fabric or carpet, excessively worn tires, cracked or broken glass, and poor-quality repairs. Your own contract controls, so read its wear section instead of relying on a general list.

What you can do about it

  • Attend the inspection if you can, and review the condition report before you sign that you received it.
  • Write down your concerns on the report. You may be asked to sign to confirm you received a copy.
  • Ask about disputes. State law or your lease may let you dispute the report, and some lessors allow a third-party appraiser both sides accept to make a binding call on excessive wear.
  • Ask about a pre-return inspection. The Fed notes that some lessors require or permit one before the scheduled end date, which gives you notice of expected charges.

Where a buyout changes things

If you keep the car, you are buying it as it sits. The wear-and-tear charges described above are charges for returning the car, so they are not part of the purchase. That does not make wear free: dings, worn tires and a stained seat are still yours to live with or repair. But it removes the risk of a surprise bill from an inspector whose standards you did not choose.

A simple way to compare

  1. Get the payoff or purchase price from the lessor, in writing.
  2. Add up the likely return costs: disposition fee plus any excess mileage and wear you expect. A pre-return inspection, if offered, turns the guess into a number.
  3. Compare buy (payoff plus taxes and fees) against return (those charges, plus the cost of whatever you drive next).

The Fed's guide also notes that on a closed-end lease you are not responsible for a shortfall between the depreciation you paid for and the car's actual depreciation, so the residual risk of a low market value sits with the lessor. That is a point in favor of returning when a car is worth less than its payoff. It is a point against when the car is worth more.

Common questions

Do I pay wear-and-tear charges if I buy my leased car?

The charges described in the Federal Reserve guide apply when you return the vehicle. If you purchase it, you are not returning it, but your contract and payoff quote control, so confirm with the lessor.

Who decides what is excessive wear?

Your lease agreement states the lessor's standard for excessive wear, and the lessor or its inspector applies it. State law or your lease may let you dispute the report.

Can I get an inspection before the lease ends?

Some lessors require or permit one before the scheduled termination date. Ask yours.
